timeline.event: Spain banned the export of merino sheep, and the crown tightly controlled access to the breed.
A selected royal consignment of merinos went to Saxony, where breeders developed extremely fine wool.
Merinos descended from a flock that Carlos III of Spain had given to the House of Orange reached New South Wales.
The US Wool Products Labeling Act was enacted, defining wool and requiring fiber content disclosure.
New Zealand's Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018 prohibited mulesing, with the ban in force from October 2018.

production.scope: global wool production, roughly 0.9% of the world fiber market

Norway's Consumer Authority warned that marketing garments with Higg MSI data could mislead, a caution relevant to single-score fiber claims.
Textile Exchange published a cashmere life cycle assessment using data from 170 herders and farmers in Mongolia and China.

timeline.event: Spun, dyed and knotted wild flax fibers were recovered from Upper Paleolithic layers at Dzudzuana Cave in Georgia, radiocarbon dated as early as about 32,000 to 26,000 years before present.
Hand hackling pins held by the Irish Linen Centre and Lisburn Museum, dated about 1850, record the combing of scutched flax into line fiber and tow.
From January 2025 the European Flax certification was renamed Masters of FLAX FIBRE, covering flax grown and scutched in Europe without irrigation.
The Alliance for European Flax-Linen and Hemp reported 38 Masters of LINEN certified companies in eight European countries in December 2025.
European scutching mills produced a record of about 190,000 tonnes of long flax fiber, up from about 116,000 tonnes in 2024, according to the Alliance.

production.figure: about 190,000 tonnes of scutched long fiber (about 116,000 tonnes in 2024)
production.scope: European scutched long flax fiber only, not a world total; short fiber and tow excluded
